title: Recreating Hardware, and the Word Everyone Gets Wrong
content:
Most FPGA retro hardware is described as emulation. It generally is not, and the distinction is not pedantic, because it determines what the thing can actually be used for.
The MiST project is the one that draws the line most carefully, and its own documentation is the best explanation of this I have read. It defines replication as FPGA code based on the actual circuitry of the original hardware, and emulation as anything using some other approximation. Then it says something that a lot of buyers of FPGA gear would rather not hear:
Currently, it’s hard to find a core that can truly be called a replica. The most widely used CPU cores, the Z80 (T80) and MC68000 (TG68K), are pure functional emulations, not replications.
So the parts people care about most are the ones that are reimplemented rather than recreated, which is worth knowing before you buy something described as cycle-accurate.
Why the FPGA is not just a faster emulator. The reason is concurrency, not clock speed.
A software emulator runs sequentially, so it has to time-slice between chips that on real hardware run at the same time: the CPU, the video chip, the sound chip, and whatever arbitrates the memory bus. That interleaving is the expensive part, and it is where approximations creep in, because getting the interleaving exactly right is very difficult and the payoff is invisible until it is not.
An FPGA is an array of logic cells wired by a hardware description. Every subsystem exists simultaneously, the way it did originally, and the chip contention that the real machine had is reproduced because the hardware is actually contending. The demo the MiST wiki uses is an Amiga 600 running a polygon demo: it stutters under emulation on a Raspberry Pi whose CPU benchmarks are a hundred times faster than the original machine, and runs smoothly on the FPGA at a fraction of the clock rate.
That is the whole argument, and it generalises past retro hardware. When your workload is genuinely parallel, throwing sequential resources at it is the wrong shape of solution, and a faster processor is not a substitute for the concurrency the original design had for free.
How the machine is actually put together. MiSTer is a Terasic DE10-Nano board built around an Intel Cyclone V SoC, which packages an FPGA together with a dual-core ARM Cortex-A9 and a gigabyte of DDR3 that both can reach. The split is clean: Linux runs on the ARM side and handles housekeeping, files, USB, networking, and the on-screen display. The FPGA runs the target machine. The target machine’s code is a Verilog or VHDL core, loaded as a .rbf file, which reconfigures the logic cells into the shape of the chips it is imitating.
The one detail I would not have guessed: most cores need an SDRAM add-on board. The DE10-Nano’s own DDR3 is unsuitable for retro memory, because its latency is too high and the ARM side is using it.
The other approach: keep the machine, add a processor. The ZX Spectrum Next does not reimplement a Z80. It implements a Z80N, an FPGA CPU that is Z80-compatible and runs four selectable speeds, in a Xilinx Artix-7. It supports the documented and undocumented opcodes, and it reproduces the contention and floating-bus behaviour of the original models, which is exactly the property that makes old software work.
The extension instructions are the elegant part. Every one is encoded as an ED prefix followed by an otherwise-unused byte, so the additions cannot conflict with any real Z80 code. MUL D,E, barrel shifts, PUSH $nn, block copy variants. Software written for a 1982 machine runs unchanged, and the extensions sit in the space the original architecture left empty.
That is a genuinely good design, and it is the same instinct as the transactional outbox: do not break the thing that already works, find the gap, and use it.
